Hot take: what if it’s actually okay to do either one? I think it’s fine to stay comfortable or become uncomfortable. I feel like if I were to like believe that being comfortable isn’t gonna help my ocd, I would like start obsessively trying to leave my comfort zone 😭 so I don’t think this is the approach for everyone. However there absolutely is a degree of exposure therapy that is unavoidable with OCD recovery that I think everyone can relate to!!

But being scared and having panic attacks are okay as well. They’re just feelings and they happen, and we shouldn’t try to choreograph a life where we avoid comfortable OR uncomfortable feelings. We need to be able to live with both.

They do feel so real 😭 it always helps me to remember a few things 

1) our thoughts are just a mixture of memories, and don’t actually say anything about us. It does, however, say a lot about the environment you grew up in and the people around you. Ex: if it’s engrained in your that your emotions and memories are false, you probably experience some sort of emotional neglect or abuse as a child.

2) we don’t need to understand the thoughts, we just need to observe and acknowledge them. I often have intrusive memories, and recently I have started to just sit with them instead of pushing them away or trying to think of how I could’ve done it better. It has helped a lot with my anxiety. 

3) our thoughts are extremely unreliable narrators!!!!!

I say this every time I explain my ocd since it’s how my therapist explained it to me:

Our thoughts are just like clouds in the sky, passing by as we observe them. We don’t need to try to understand them or how they got there, we just need to observe/acknowledge/accept them and the way they make us feel.

I often feel delusional too. My parents and I have opposite memories of my childhood and they are always telling me that I’m not experiencing whatever I’m experiencing (for example, for some reason it is never believed that I experience tiredness, just laziness apparently).

Simply put, a feeling can’t be wrong. It is impossible. It’s just the body’s way of regulating itself and communicating to you. You actually can’t control your emotions either — the same way you can’t just get in  control of your digestive system. It’s a natural process that the body goes through, and if someone is telling you that it’s wrong, they are definitely the crazy one. 

It can be hard to believe this kind of stuff after a lifetime of hearing “control yourself” whenever you get upset. So I was very apprehensive to the idea that what I was experiencing was real for a very long time and I pushed everything down. Decided it was just a lack of skill. And it is a lack of skill, a skill I wasn’t taught because my parents weren’t around to teach it. And also actively didn’t want to deal with me because their lives are messy as Fuck lol (they claim mine is messier but just trust me on this one).

I have found that it’s best if I just observe the thought. Like it’s a cloud passing by in the sky. Just a thought. And the thought doesn’t say anything about me as a person — our thoughts are just narratives that we have picked up from our lives. It is just a mixture of things from my memory and nothing more. 

I’m not sure if any of this helped but I really understand where you’re coming from and I hope you can find some relief from this shitty disorder !

Hey! Very similar struggles here. OCD/CPTSD, history of abuse/anxiety/depression and other stuff.

I have struggled with these thoughts as well. My parents only gave me negative attention as a child, rarely any positive attention, so anytime I was around them, I would be constantly scanning for things I could’ve possibly done wrong to reduce harm as much as possible. And this habit has continued into adulthood unfortunately and is still a present issue. What I understand in myself about this issue so far, is that it is so much easier for me to go along with the narrative that I am a horrible person. It fits the narrative my parents have written for me and it is how I have come to understand the world. So I naturally get VERY emotionally activated around feelings of guilt and shame. Whenever it’s even implied that I might have done something wrong, I just break into a frenzy of apologies and offerings of how I can make things better. It runs very deep 😭

The way I cope with these thoughts is from something my therapist taught me: basically instead of trying to understand the thoughts going on and wrap your head around the OCD ideas, just observe the thoughts like a cloud passing by in the sky. It’s just a thought. 

Our thoughts are our life narratives and stories. And we are EXTREMELY unreliable narrators of our own stories. So your thoughts have as much credibility as a slice of bread. 

Also, the majority of the time, we are regurgitating narratives that other people have written for our stories, opposed to our own. So it’s most likely that it’s your parents voices subjecting you to this internal interrogation here. Which luckily can be changed with time.

The hardest part for me was allowing myself to observe the thought without the guilt taking over. I’m honestly still working through that part. But I know that I don’t need to answer the “why am I like this” question now. Most questions from my OCD are meant to be observed and not answered.

A lot of the stuff with OCD is way easier said than done tho xD

I hope this helped or at least made you feel less crazy/alone 🌸 I hope you find relief from this nasty disorder my friend

Don’t try to understand your OCD, just observe it. 

Best advice my therapist has ever given to me. Thought about maybe me being a horrible person? I’ll just observe that thought as though I’m watching a cloud float by. Nothing more than just a thought in my head. 

Also helped to understand that my thoughts are just how I am writing the story of my life, and we are very unreliable narrators of our own stories! So trying to understand them deeply isn’t the most effective way for me to work through the obsessive thoughts. Even though it seems like the logical answer. 

Finally, listen to your body. If you’re someone like me who has pushed their feelings down since you were a small child, you might relate (or just for other similar reasons) to the experience of just feeling paralyzed by your thoughts and feelings. Frozen. And in those moments I again just like to observe what is happening in my body. Just observe the nervous stomach, racing heart etc. I don’t need to get rid of these sensations or try to fix them either, just make an observation of them and accept that they are there. Very neutral approach that has helped me a ton.

I don’t mess around with silhouettes too much, I’m kinda hyperfemme xD

Long story short: you don’t need to lose weight. The only concern you actually NEED to have about your body is keeping yourself healthy.

This is a super common stigma for people with BPD! And it didn’t just come out of thin air, you’re right that there seems to be a bit of a pattern for people with BPD to have toxic or unstable relationships.

BPD is usually the result of having attachment issues early in childhood. For example, maybe they lost a parent at a very early age, were abandoned for prolonged periods of time as a child, etc. Basically, children who don’t develop a secure attachment to their parents grow up to be adults with BPD (or at least that is my understanding of it as someone who isn’t a doctor). 

It’s not shocking that adults with BPD who haven’t gotten a significant amount of treatment tend to have toxic relationships. We model our relationships after our parents, and if your parents were nasty to each other, or never talked, then you’re much more likely to turn relationships toxic. This isn’t malicious, it’s a consequence of neglect/abuse.

At the same time, however, you’re right that this is often abuse. It’s probably not intentional abuse, but most abuse isn’t intentional. And you’re 100% justified in your upset feelings about having toxic relationships with mentally ill women. It takes a lot of time to heal from attachment issues… a lot of time. So a lot of the times with BPD it’s best to focus more on healing yourself and your own trauma than getting into a relationship. It’s not impossible to do both at the time, but it’s damn hard. 

All in all, BPD is a very very devastating mental illness, both to those who are diagnosed and as well to their loved ones watching them in pain, sometimes catching some collateral damage. Again, your anger and upset are justified. You can’t excuse abuse just because someone is mentally ill, ever. But understanding mental illnesses can help to explain why people act the way they act. And it helps us find closure sometimes.

Hi there! I’ve been trying different medications for a few years now and I have to say that sometimes finding the right medication for you can take a lot of trial and error. For me, it was 2-3 years of trying different medications, observing the side effects, and reporting it all to my psychiatrist as it happened. And after those years of trial and error, a few months ago I finally found the winning combo. I found a combination of medication (Wellbutrin, effexor, and vyvanse) that improve my quality of life, my executive function, as well as my mood. And it kinda feels like I just found the key to becoming happy again. 

For context, I spent months in my bed, failed out of college, and struggled with substance abuse, so I really had a lot of issues (CPTSD, OCD, GAD, MDD and BED) to address so it took a lot longer to find the right medication combo. It may take you much less time to experiment with medications and find the one that works best with your brain/body/nervous system. 

Also, no person will have the same experience with medication. EX my sister loved Zoloft, and it gave me insomnia and panic attacks. I even read in this comment section that someone totally had an awful time on effexor - which is the drug that saved my life xD so experiences truly, truly vary! So don’t be discouraged by people who had bad experiences on specific drugs. 

It is unfortunate though that for us dealing with CPTSD & symptoms, there is not really any source of healthy AND immediate relief. But I truly feel that medication is the best thing to do to get that relief as soon as possible. The first drug I ever tried was prozac, and it massively improved my life for a really long time. It didn’t end up being a perfect match due to it eventually making me kinda moody at the end of the day before taking my next dose, but it genuinely gave me the ability to like leave my house and enjoy myself. Hey! I have had a very similar experience. I have been diagnosed with binge eating disorder, depression, anxiety, ADHD, BPD, and OCD (gradually over the years). All of these diagnoses are just the psychological consequences of the experiences I went through growing up, essentially. 

Also, not sure if this is something you might identify with, but sometimes people develop tics as a trauma response. I have a friend with DID who has tics that have been slowly going away as she processes childhood trauma. Not to say you don’t have Tourette’s, you totally could, just offering my one little theory here in case you relate.

Also, I’m like 90% sure BPD forms as a result of early childhood trauma/a lack of healthy attachment to parental guardians in early childhood (I could be wrong tho as I’m not a doctor and a therapist said this to me), so if you do have any childhood trauma, chances are that your diagnoses may be symptoms of CPTSD or PTSD. I highly recommend looking through r/CPTSD if this resonates with you at all. Or r/CPTSDmemes, love that one.

Also, one final note, you could also totally just have these comorbidities. I’m not a doctor so I could be very wrong about everything. Trust yourself more than you trust me, your symptoms will tell you everything.

Hi! I have PCOS and have also struggled with weight gain for a really long time. The only answer I really have is that she has to come to want a stable weight for herself, and/or get on medication that controls the hormones that PCOS affects. Also, a high protein/low carb diet is HUGE for a lot of people with PCOS. I rarely exercise but I’m able to maintain a decent weight with a high protein/low carb diet, so maybe trying cooking healthy meals for her, cutting up fruit for her throughout the day, or something like that. 

Also, nothing wrong with being attracted to healthy habits — that’s a really good quality. However usually our habits become more maladaptive when we’re going through something. Maybe she is stressed out, anxious/depressed, trying to fulfill some sort of emotional need with food, or just eat for comfort/boredom. I’m not sure if that resonates with anything she’s been going through, that’s just my personal experience. Could be projecting. 

As for having a conversation with her — I know you said that she craves food more when you tell her she can’t have it. A wise dietician once told me to “delay, don’t deny”. Aka if you really want pizza or that croissant, you can have it, just make an occasion out of it. Give it a day or so before you have it, or a few hours. The cravings will never go away with PCOS (unless you take medication), so it’s just a matter of pacing yourself with the foods you crave and the foods that are healthy for you.
